world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bukusu (buku1249) is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items are non-yielding for word stress. Mutonyi 1992 (OSU WPL 41, open on the OSU Knowledge Bank, already held by the project and re-read) is about moraic structure and compensatory lengthening; it contains no stress/accent statement at all. Philippson's 1991/1992 Paris 5 Thèse d'État on tone and accent in East African Bantu is print/microfiche only (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; SUDOC holdings at Paris-UPCité, CTLES, Montpellier, Strasbourg BNU, Paris BIS; not on HAL); its abstract describes a ~30-language continuum from pure tone (Kikuyu) to demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili) without naming Bukusu, and the open 1998 Faits de langues derivative (downloaded from Persée, saved as per-page text) never mentions Bukusu or Luyia. No first-hand statement of Bukusu word stress was read in this search of works with stress in the title; the only bearing on the question remains the second-hand Google Books snippet already logged by the earlier reading (Downing 2005b: Gikuyu and Bukusu 'have no reported stress'; Hubbard 1994: penultimate syllable receives extra duration), which was not opened as full text. Priority for acquisition: Philippson thesis medium (survey may include Bukusu but the abstract does not show it); the better targets for a first-hand Bukusu prosody statement remain de Blois 1975 (RMCA, print), Austen 1974 (SAL Suppl. 5) and Mutonyi 2000 (OSU PhD, ProQuest) from the earlier reading. All downloaded records are and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: Mutonyi 1996:77-78: "Bukusu, which has preserved the Proto-Bantu H(igh)/Low lexical tone contrast in its verbs, displays classic tense-determined tone alternations ... it will be shown that there are at least three kinds of H tones involved. These include two lexical H tones, which are the stem H and object prefix H tones, a tense-aspect imposed melodic H, and a phrasal H tone inserted between any two adjacent words." Downing 2005b (snippet): "... continuum of stress systems, from languages like Swahili (G42) which have uncontroversial word stress, to languages like Gikuyu (E51) and Bukusu (J31c), which have no reported stress, to the Southern Bantu languages illustrated in (2) and (3) above, which lie somewhere in between these two extremes."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Mutonyi 1996 (held: the quoted passage is verbatim at p.77 (sec. 0, 'Bukusu, which has preserved the Proto-Bantu H(igh)/Low lexical tone contrast in its verbs, displays classic tense-determined tone alternations..' and '.. at least three kinds of H tones involved. These include two lexical H tones, which are the stem H and object prefix H tones, a tense-aspect imposed melodic H, and a phrasal H tone inserted between any two adjacent words'); p.78 sec. 1 repeats the H/Low contrast; p.81 'prominent - i.e. by assigning it a H tone'; p.109 'a prepausal H either retracts or deletes depending on the length of the penultimate syllable'. The words stress/accent do n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bukusu is described first-hand only as a tone language (privative H vs toneless roots, melodic and phrasal H tones, mora as TBU); no accessible primary description states a word-stress or accent position, and Downing (2005b), who did fieldwork-based work on Bukusu reduplication, characterises Bukusu as a language with 'no reported stress'. Hubbard 1994 (snippet only) reports extra phonetic duration on the penultimate syllable in her Bukusu measurements, i.e. possible phrase-level penultimate lengthening, unverified.
new_statements.exceptions: none; Mutonyi 1996:109 notes a prepausal H retracts or deletes depending on penult length (tonal, not stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern verbs in isolation and in phrases (phrasal H between words). The 'no reported stress' remark is a typological aside in a survey-style chapter, not a dedicated prosodic description; the deciding primary works (Mutonyi 2000, de Blois 1975, Austen 1974a/b) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Bukusu/Lubukusu (JE31c, buku1249) of Bungoma, western Kenya; Mutonyi's data are his own (native speaker) dialect. Hubbard's and Downing's Bukusu data also derive from work with Mutonyi. No dialect mismatch; Tachoni and Gisu/Masaaba are separate glottocodes and were not used.

sources.note: First-hand tonal description (native-speaker linguist): Bukusu 'has preserved the Proto-Bantu H/Low lexical tone contrast in its verbs' (p.77-78); lexical stem H, object-prefix H, tense-imposed melodic H and a phrasal H; p.81 uses 'prominent' only in the sense 'assigned a H tone'; p.109 a prepausal H 'either retracts or deletes depending on the length of the penultimate syllable'. The words stress/accent do not occur; no statement on word stress.

sources.citation: Mutonyi, Nasiombe (1992). Cs and Vs or moras: the case of Bukusu prosodic structure. Ohio State University Working Papers in Linguistics 41: 46-84.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Our task in this paper is not to try and resolve the dilemma faced by phonologists in this regard, but rather to examine a few prosodic structures in Bukusu which seem to favor the moraic theory over CV phonology. ... In section 3, I adduce evidence for the four processes which trigger compensatory lengthening (CL)
sources.note: Nothing. 'Prosodic structure' in the title means moraic/skeletal structure: the paper treats compensatory lengthening from glide formation, vowel contraction, pre-nasal-consonant lengthening and prefix haplology, and touches tone only incidentally (fn. on H placement on stem moras, falling tone on lengthened preprefix vowels). The strings 'stress', 'accent', 'penult' and 'prominen' do not occur anywhere in the text layer.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. ... Une trentaine de langues en tout sont utilisées comme exemples. Enfin, on établit systématiquement les correspondances prosodiques entre chacune des langues concernées et le bantu commun et on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. [tr.: These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), with every intermediate case represented. ... Some thirty languages in all are used as examples. Finally ... the hypothesis is proposed that the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative accent on the penult serving as a domain limit for tone association.]
